tests.description: The order that makes the log readable.
tests.key: useAdvancePhase › writes the note before it moves the phase

tests.description: Selection inside a card's own controls is not the board's to suppress — the composer is a textarea, and text you cannot select in one is a regression traded for the fix rather than a fix.
tests.key: useBoardCamera and text selection › leaves selection alone for a press inside a no-pan subtree

tests.description: A cancelled gesture — the pointer leaving the window, a touch interrupted by a system gesture — must not leave the page permanently unselectable. `onPointerCancel` is the same handler, so this pins the wiring rather than the restore itself.
tests.key: useBoardCamera and text selection › restores selection when the gesture is cancelled rather than released

tests.description: The reported complaint: a drag across a card paints a selection highlight that trails the cursor, because the browser reads the pan as a select. The lock goes on at pointerdown rather than at the pan threshold. Three pixels in, the browser already has a selection drag in flight and clearing its ranges leaves the anchor for it to keep extending from — so a test that only checked the state after a threshold-crossing move would pass over the very placement that does not work.
tests.key: useBoardCamera and text selection › turns text selection off while a board gesture is running

tests.description: A hand tremor during a click is a click, not a pan. Below the threshold the board must not creep — a board that nudges every time you answer a card feels broken in a way that is hard to name.
tests.key: useBoardCamera panning › does not pan for movement below the threshold

tests.description: Only the primary button drags; a right-click is a context menu.
tests.key: useBoardCamera panning › ignores a non-primary button

tests.description: The bug, stated as the behaviour that must hold. A press and release with no movement in between must leave the camera untouched AND must never call setPointerCapture — the capture is what swallowed the click, so its absence is the actual assertion, not the unchanged camera.
tests.key: useBoardCamera panning › never captures the pointer on a click that does not move

tests.description: Past the threshold it is a drag, and only THEN is the pointer captured — so the gesture survives the cursor leaving the element, without having cost anyone a click.
tests.key: useBoardCamera panning › pans and captures once the pointer has travelled far enough

tests.description: A drag beginning inside a card's own controls belongs to the control. A textarea you cannot select text in because the board panned away underneath is the same class of bug as the unclickable card.
tests.key: useBoardCamera panning › refuses to start a drag from inside a control

tests.description: The delta is divided by the current scale so the board tracks the cursor by the same SCREEN distance however far out you are zoomed. Without it a drag zoomed out crawls and a drag zoomed in throws the board off-screen.
tests.key: useBoardCamera panning › tracks the cursor identically at every zoom level

tests.description: A focus that asks for an out-of-range zoom is clamped like any other, so "frame everything" on a huge board cannot push the camera past the floor.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › clamps a zoom asked for through focusOn

tests.description: Safari does not only send ctrl+wheel for a trackpad pinch; it also emits its own gesture events, and an unprevented gesturestart still hands Safari its page zoom. Preventing the wheel alone leaves the bug half-fixed there.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › consumes Safari gesture events so the page does not scale

tests.description: The reported bug: a trackpad pinch over the board zoomed the whole PAGE. The board's wheel handler was a React `onWheel` prop, and React attaches `wheel` passively at the root — so preventDefault could never fire and the browser applied its own zoom on top. The assertion is `defaultPrevented`, not the camera: the camera already moved before the fix, and the page zoomed anyway.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › consumes a trackpad pinch instead of letting the page zoom

tests.description: Flying to a card moves the camera and may change the zoom in the same commit — the two are one piece of state precisely so they cannot tear.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › focuses on a point, optionally changing zoom with it

tests.description: The clamp at both ends. Past the floor the board is a few pixels of noise with no way back; past the ceiling one card fills the screen and the shape of the thinking — the entire point of the board — is gone.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › holds the zoom inside its limits at both ends

tests.description: Zoom must never invert. A negative or zero scale flips or collapses the whole transformed layer, and every coordinate that divides by it explodes.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › never lets the scale reach zero or go negative

tests.description: A plain wheel is a two-finger scroll, which the board reads as a pan — and it too must be consumed, because the board is a canvas and every wheel event over it belongs to the board rather than to the page behind it.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › pans rather than zooms on a plain wheel, and consumes that too

tests.description: Swallowing the gesture is only half the fix. A handler that prevents the default and then does nothing would pass the test above while leaving the board frozen under a pinch, which is a worse bug than the one being fixed.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › scales the board when a pinch is consumed

tests.description: The listeners belong to the surface, so unmounting must take them with it. A board that keeps swallowing wheel events after it is gone would freeze scrolling on whatever replaced it.
tests.key: useBoardCamera zooming › stops consuming wheel events once the board unmounts

tests.description: An unmounted map must not leave a timer running.
tests.key: useBoundedWait › clears its timer on unmount

tests.description: Inactive means there is nothing being waited on, so no clock runs.
tests.key: useBoundedWait › never elapses while inactive

tests.description: A round that goes back to being unanswered — the person pressed Edit — is not still waiting, and must not carry its old elapsed time forward.
tests.key: useBoundedWait › resets when the wait stops being active

tests.description: The one that matters for a live map: a new round arrived, so the page is reaching for the NEXT thing and the wait starts over rather than being already expired.
tests.key: useBoundedWait › restarts the wait when the reset key changes

tests.description: Nothing has elapsed at the moment the wait begins.
tests.key: useBoundedWait › starts at zero

tests.description: It reports a step rather than a running total: re-rendering the map column once a frame to move a decision that flips once would be pure waste.
tests.key: useBoundedWait › stays at zero until the limit, then reports the limit

tests.description: The callback is re-created on every render of the component that owns it, so a hook that captured the first one would keep calling a stale closure — moving to a question chosen from a board several answers out of date.
tests.key: useDelayedAdvance › calls the newest callback, not the one captured when it was armed

tests.description: Someone who takes hold of the board has overruled the automation. Moving the view out from under a person who is doing something is the failure this cancel exists to prevent.
tests.key: useDelayedAdvance › does not move on if it was cancelled first

tests.description: A pending jump firing after the board has gone would move a camera that no longer exists.
tests.key: useDelayedAdvance › drops a pending move when the board unmounts

tests.description: Answering two cards quickly must not queue two jumps — the second answer replaces the first one's pending move rather than adding to it.
tests.key: useDelayedAdvance › re-arming replaces the pending move rather than queueing another

tests.description: The pause is the point. Moving the instant the answer is recorded takes the card away before the person has seen their own words land on it, which reads as the board having eaten the answer.
tests.key: useDelayedAdvance › waits before moving on, so the card can turn over first

tests.description: The keyboard route out, which is the only one a person navigating without a pointer has.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › dismisses on Escape

tests.description: The ordinary dismissal: a pointer lands somewhere that is not the overlay.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › dismisses on a pointer down outside the element

tests.description: Nothing is open, so nothing is listening — every one of these surfaces spends most of its life closed, and a closed menu firing a dismissal would be a callback nobody asked for.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › does not listen while closed

tests.description: Escape is the exit, not every key. A person typing into a field inside the overlay must not close it on the first letter.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › ignores keys other than Escape

tests.description: The half that makes it usable rather than a trap: clicking the overlay's own contents must not close the thing being clicked.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › leaves the overlay open for a pointer down inside it

tests.description: Unmounting is the other way an overlay goes away — navigating off the map while the panel is open — and it must clean up the same way closing does.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › stops listening on unmount

tests.description: The teardown. Without it every open/close cycle would leave another listener on the document, and the callback would fire once per cycle the surface had ever been through.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › stops listening once it closes

tests.description: A ref that has not attached yet cannot contain anything, so the pointer is outside by definition rather than a crash on `.contains` of null.
tests.key: useDismissOnOutside › treats a null ref as outside rather than throwing

tests.description: Closing it now, and recording that it was closed. Both halves matter: the second is what stops it coming back on the next map.
tests.key: useDismissedOnce › hides it once, and remembers

tests.description: Two notes must not dismiss each other.
tests.key: useDismissedOnce › remembers each key separately

tests.description: The failure that decides the direction of the whole hook. A private window, cleared site data, or a browser set to block site data can make the read THROW — and showing an instruction twice is a far smaller failure than never showing it at all, so a throw has to leave it visible.
tests.key: useDismissedOnce › shows it anyway when the browser refuses to be read

tests.description: The ordinary first visit. It is shown only after the effect runs, never on the first render — server and client must agree, and only the client can know what the browser remembers.
tests.key: useDismissedOnce › shows the thing to someone who has never dismissed it

tests.description: The second visit, which is the whole reason this is remembered at all.
tests.key: useDismissedOnce › stays hidden on a later visit

tests.description: Closing has to work even when the closing cannot be recorded. Someone meeting the note once more on another visit is not worth a broken button.
tests.key: useDismissedOnce › still closes when the browser refuses to be written to

tests.description: Nothing changed, so there is nothing to react to.
tests.key: useFollowColumn › does not scroll on a re-render that changes neither input

tests.description: The regression that shipped once: StrictMode double-invokes effects on mount, so a "have I run yet" flag gets consumed by the first invocation and the second one scrolls. Seeding from mount-time values means neither invocation sees a transition.
tests.key: useFollowColumn › does not scroll on mount, even when the effect runs twice

tests.description: THE COURTESY. Someone who scrolled up to re-read round one is reading, and a round arriving must not drag them back down.
tests.key: useFollowColumn › leaves a reader alone who has scrolled up

tests.description: And it picks them back up when they return to the bottom, rather than giving up on following for the rest of the session.
tests.key: useFollowColumn › resumes following once the reader returns to the bottom

tests.description: A round arriving is the page reacting, and that is what earns a scroll.
tests.key: useFollowColumn › scrolls when a new round arrives

tests.description: The moment the last answer goes in, the map reaches for the next row — and the column follows it down. This is "the app moves first" as a scroll.
tests.key: useFollowColumn › scrolls when the round completes and the page starts reaching

tests.description: The map renders in isolated scenarios with no scroll container measured; reading the position must not throw there.
tests.key: useFollowColumn › survives being asked for a position with no container

tests.description: The write goes out in the shape the bridge takes: the answer keyed by node id, and the question it belongs to alongside it.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › hands the writer the answer and the question it belongs to

tests.description: A failure on one question must not disturb another that succeeded.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › leaves other answers standing when one write fails

tests.description: An isolated scenario has no exchange to write to. The map must still read correctly; it simply offers no way to answer.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › offers no way to answer when there is no writer

tests.description: The answers already in the log are what a reloaded page shows.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › reads the answers already in the log

tests.description: Editing an answer is posting another one, so the newer value must win on the card as well as in the log.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › replaces an earlier answer with a newer one for the same question

tests.description: With nothing answered, every card is still asking.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › reports no answers for an empty log

tests.description: The optimistic case: the answer is on the card before the write resolves.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › shows an answer immediately, before the write completes

tests.description: The rollback. A failed write must not leave the card claiming an answer that was never recorded.
tests.key: useMapAnswers › takes the answer back off the card when the write fails

tests.description: Cancelling ends THIS round's countdown, not the feature. The next round has to arrive with a fresh one or the board silently stops ending itself for the rest of the session.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › arms again for the next round after a hold

tests.description: The number is the whole point of counting down in the open rather than firing at once — someone has to be able to see how long they have.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › counts down in whole seconds once armed

tests.description: Ticks keep arriving after expiry until the caller disarms. Firing on each one would write a fresh note onto the shared log four times a second.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › does not fire again on the ticks after it expires

tests.description: The headline behaviour: left alone, the round ends on its own.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › fires once when the countdown runs out

tests.description: The race the tick's ref re-read exists for: a hold landing between two scheduled ticks must make the already-queued tick a no-op, not end a round the person just cancelled.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › ignores a tick already scheduled when the hold landed

tests.description: THE PRODUCTION FAILURE THIS HOOK IS SHAPED AROUND. The board calls router.refresh() on every revision bump, so an agent writing anything at all re-renders it with a fresh onExpire identity and restarts the effect. Held in state instead of a ref, the deadline would reset on each of those and the round would never end while a partner was working.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › keeps counting across re-renders that change the callback identity

tests.description: Nothing counts down until the board says the round is finished. This is what keeps a board with open questions on it completely still.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › reports nothing while disarmed

tests.description: "A visible cancel" is the promise the countdown is allowed to exist on. If holding open did not actually hold, the automation would be a thing done TO the person rather than for them.
tests.key: useSelfEndingRound › stops for good once the round is held open

tests.description: These three are what the contribution affordances post. Narrowing this set would silently drop a person's contribution on the floor.
tests.key: user-writable event kinds › accepts the three kinds a person can contribute

tests.description: The agent's own kinds are minted by the tools. Accepting one from the browser would let a page forge the other side of the conversation.
tests.key: user-writable event kinds › refuses the kinds only an agent may write

tests.description: A tool whose fields are all optional must accept an omitted payload rather than forcing the agent to send an empty object.
tests.key: validateToolInput › accepts a missing payload for a tool that needs no arguments

tests.description: The happy path returns the parsed input, so defaults and coercions the schema applies are what actually reach the server.
tests.key: validateToolInput › accepts input that fits the tool and hands back the parsed value

tests.description: The message has to name the offending field, or the agent can only guess at what to change.
tests.key: validateToolInput › names the field that did not fit

tests.description: A required field left out is the other common agent mistake.
tests.key: validateToolInput › rejects a call missing a required field

tests.description: The controlled vocabulary is what keeps the map drawable: a kind the map cannot render must never reach the database.
tests.key: validateToolInput › rejects a node kind the map cannot draw

tests.description: The phase drives the nav; one outside the loop would leave the workspace with no step marked active.
tests.key: validateToolInput › rejects a phase outside the loop

tests.description: A name the catalog does not know must come back as an answer, not a throw, or one bad call takes down the whole binding.
tests.key: validateToolInput › rejects a tool the catalog does not define

tests.description: Answering closes the question. Both halves are the same act, and the answer is the half worth a row.
tests.key: visibleEvents › hides the node.updated that an answer closed

tests.description: ask_user writes the question nodes AND announces them. Showing both would report one act twice, and the bare adds are the half nobody can act on.
tests.key: visibleEvents › hides the question nodes that a question.asked announced

tests.description: An open-question node put on the map WITHOUT an ask_user is a real contribution — nothing announced it, so nothing may hide it.
tests.key: visibleEvents › keeps a question node that nothing announced

tests.description: A user update that is not the answer's own close — a relabel, say — is a real edit and is not bookkeeping.
tests.key: visibleEvents › keeps a user update that is not the answer close

tests.description: The suppression is narrow on purpose: an AGENT closing the same node is a separate act by the other side and must still be reported.
tests.key: visibleEvents › keeps an agent update to a node the person answered

tests.description: Lax, not Strict: the saved-map list is reached by following an ordinary link, and Strict would drop the cookie on exactly that navigation — the returning visitor would land on the day-one screen holding a valid cookie.
tests.key: visitorCookieOptions › is SameSite lax so following a link still carries it

tests.description: The reason the cookie exists at all is to say which browser owns a map, so nothing in the page may read it. httpOnly is what makes that structural rather than a convention nobody enforces.
tests.key: visitorCookieOptions › is httpOnly so no client code can read it

tests.description: But NOT secure in development, or http://localhost would never receive it and the whole feature would look broken on the machine it is built on.
tests.key: visitorCookieOptions › is not secure in development so http localhost still works

tests.description: Deployed, the cookie must not travel in clear text.
tests.key: visitorCookieOptions › is secure in production

tests.description: Scoped to the whole site and long-lived. A path-scoped cookie would be missing on `/map/<id>`, where the Boards menu reads the same list, and a session cookie would make "pick up where you left off" mean "until you close the tab".
tests.key: visitorCookieOptions › is site-wide and long-lived

tests.description: The whole point of handing the cursor back: re-parking with it must not re-deliver work the agent has already been given.
tests.key: waitForNewMap › does not re-deliver a map through the cursor it handed back

tests.description: The wake path, and the reason the feature exists at all.
tests.key: waitForNewMap › releases when a map is created during the wait

tests.description: hasBrief is what decides read_brief over read_map downstream, so it has to be right for both shapes of map.
tests.key: waitForNewMap › reports whether each map was started from a brief

tests.description: The check-first guarantee: a map created between the agent's last call and this one is already waiting, and a waiter that subscribed before checking would sleep straight through it.
tests.key: waitForNewMap › returns immediately when a map already exists after the cursor

tests.description: One wait can cover several submissions, and creation order is the order an agent should work them in.
tests.key: waitForNewMap › returns several maps in creation order when they arrive together

tests.description: A timeout must RESOLVE and must carry a usable cursor — an agent looping on this sees the empty case far more often than the full one.
tests.key: waitForNewMap › times out cleanly with a usable cursor when nobody starts anything

tests.description: The agent's own writes must not wake it — otherwise an agent that posts a note wakes itself and never actually waits for the person.
tests.key: waitForUserActivity › does not wake on the agent’s own writes

tests.description: An event may already be waiting. A waiter that subscribed before checking would sleep through it and time out with the answer already on disk.
tests.key: waitForUserActivity › returns immediately when the person already acted

tests.description: The timeout must RESOLVE, not hang and not throw. This is the guarantee an earlier unref'd-deadline bug broke: the promise simply never settled.
tests.key: waitForUserActivity › times out cleanly with a resume cursor when nobody acts

tests.description: The wake path: a user write during the wait must be delivered.
tests.key: waitForUserActivity › wakes and returns the user’s events when they act during the wait

tests.description: This is the string every codeyam preview and captured scenario shows. It has to read as an expected condition, not as a failure.
tests.key: webMcpUnavailableReason › names the iframe

tests.description: Each reason names a different fix, so they must not collapse into one generic "unavailable" the person cannot act on.
tests.key: webMcpUnavailableReason › names the insecure context

tests.description: Naming the version requirement is the difference between a person knowing what to do next and assuming the page is broken.
tests.key: webMcpUnavailableReason › names the missing browser agent

tests.description: A bound page must return null, since the UI shows this string only when there is genuinely something wrong to report.
tests.key: webMcpUnavailableReason › reports nothing to explain when the page is bound

tests.description: The security gates are checked before the agent gate, so an insecure page is told to fix that first rather than being sent hunting for a browser.
tests.key: webMcpUnavailableReason › reports the security problem first when several apply

tests.description: Most projects have no `stack.local.json` yet, so the block has to be created rather than merged into on the first provisioning run.

tests.description: A trailing newline keeps the file well-formed for anything that appends to it and keeps its diffs clean.
tests.key: withCodeyamEnv › ends with a newline

tests.description: This is a per-developer overrides file. Dropping a sibling key, or another env variable beside DATABASE_URL, would silently discard their config.
tests.key: withCodeyamEnv › keeps other keys and other env variables

tests.description: A file that does not parse contributes nothing to codeyam's lookup anyway, so writing a valid one beats refusing and leaving the URL unrecorded.
tests.key: withCodeyamEnv › starts over from an unparseable file rather than refusing to write

tests.description: Route handlers on dynamic segments take a second context argument, and the wrapper has to hand both through unchanged.
tests.key: withFailure › forwards every argument to the handler

tests.description: Development gets the one command that fixes it, and the column that named the problem. This is what the scenarios show.
tests.key: withFailure › includes the fix and the diagnosis in development

tests.description: An unrecognised failure is by definition one nobody anticipated, so the wrapper says nothing it has not been taught to say.
tests.key: withFailure › leaks nothing internal for an ordinary error

tests.description: A route's own 400 must survive: the wrapper covers the unanticipated throw, not the faults a handler already decided how to report.
tests.key: withFailure › leaves a handler-authored failure alone

tests.description: A handler that answers is not the wrapper's business — status and body come back exactly as written, including a deliberate non-2xx.
tests.key: withFailure › passes a successful response through untouched

tests.description: The terminal keeps the whole thing. Swallowing the original would trade one unreadable failure for an invisible one.
tests.key: withFailure › still writes the original error to the terminal

tests.description: The reported case, from the route's side: a throw becomes a 500 that is still JSON, so the browser has something it can read.
tests.key: withFailure › turns a thrown database drift into a readable JSON 500

tests.description: The check script writes to a path whose directory may not exist yet, and a first generation into a fresh clone has no evals directory at all.
tests.key: writeEvalToolsSchema › creates missing parent directories

tests.description: Regenerating over a stale file must replace it wholesale — a partial overwrite would leave trailing bytes from the previous, longer fixture.
tests.key: writeEvalToolsSchema › overwrites an existing file rather than appending

tests.description: The count is what the emitter reports to the operator; deriving it from the catalog rather than from the caller is what keeps that line honest.
tests.key: writeEvalToolsSchema › returns the number of tools written

tests.description: The bytes on disk are the ones the eval CLI reads, so they must be the serializer's output and nothing else.
tests.key: writeEvalToolsSchema › writes the serialized fixture to the given path
